correctness.finding: PASS. In the linear Nakayama case every projective contains each simple at most once, so each Hom(I_i,P_j) has dimension at most one and F(A)<=n^2. In the cyclic quasi-hereditary case, rotating a simple of projective dimension two and using the standard Kupisch criterion forces the endpoint plateau r_1=...=r_p and p<=n. This bounds every projective and injective length by 2n-1, hence each Hom dimension by at most two. The plateau and endpoint bounds then force any source with length>n to have top S_1 and any target supporting a double Hom to be P_1; the terminal-segment condition leaves only I_R=P_1 as a possible double pair. Thus F(A)<=n^2+1. For the displayed extremal Kupisch series every one of the n^2 pairs has a nonzero map and I_{n-1}=P_1 has the unique second map. I independently enumerated cyclic Kupisch series for n=2,3,4,5 under the projective-dimension-two criterion and obtained maxima 5,10,17,26 exactly.

originality.finding: PASS. The 2020 MathOverflow question explicitly conjectures the observed maxima n^2+1 and has no posted solution supplying this proof. The July 2026 paper Bounds on Frobenius dimension was obtained in full; it proves bounds in terms of the total vector-space dimension, classifies the global equality case, and gives formulas for low-dimensional and truncated path algebras, but it does not state the submitted extremal theorem for quasi-hereditary Nakayama algebras with n simples. The Marczinzik--Rubey--Stump and Uematsu--Yamagata results used in the proof supply the quasi-hereditary/Kupisch criteria and are prior input. Targeted searches found no later solution of the exact n^2+1 Nakayama question.

scientific_value.finding: PASS. The theorem resolves a concrete six-year-old extremal question with a sharp closed formula for every n and a transparent structural explanation: quasi-heredity permits at most one double injective-projective Hom. The extremal family is explicit. The scope is appropriately restricted to the standard connected basic algebraically closed setting.

limitations: The theorem is for connected basic finite-dimensional Nakayama algebras over an algebraically closed field.
It relies on established quasi-hereditary/projective-dimension criteria rather than reproving their classification theory.
It answers the extremal quasi-hereditary question only, not the separate global-dimension lower-bound question from the same MathOverflow post.
